kicker: In a gold rush, the shovel sellers get rich first. The AI boom is the same, and the shovels here are chips.
summary: Every question you ask AI runs on chips, mostly NVIDIA chips. The chip seller gets paid first, then puts money back into the very customers who buy its chips.

quiz.q: Other companies already have powerful chips. Why is NVIDIA still hard to replace?
options: NVIDIA chips are 10 times faster than any rival's
AI code is written on CUDA; switching means rewriting
NVIDIA owns more chip factories than anyone in the world
AI companies signed contracts to buy only NVIDIA chips ever
quiz.explain: NVIDIA doesn't win through factories (TSMC makes its chips) but through CUDA: programming tools that run only on NVIDIA chips, which the whole industry has written code on since 2006.

gardeners.label: A thousand spouts
gardeners.art: A terraced hill like a bonsai tray under a low full moon: 25 curved rows of 40 moss beds each, a bamboo gutter along every lip with a little spout over every bed. Front left, a paper gardener stands on a stepping stone by a stone lantern, his watering can on a rock beside him; on the crest, the bamboo valve at the head of the gutters meets the spring.
gardeners.hint: Drag to turn the tray. Touch the watering can, then pull the bamboo valve on the crest.
gardeners.group: Two ways to water the same garden
gardeners.oneAria: Water with one can (CPU): a few strong cores doing one job after another
gardeners.manyAria: Water with a thousand bamboo spouts (GPU): each spout is a small core, a thousand working at once

insight.text: Each bamboo spout is one GPU core: a thousand water together, so AI's billions of tiny sums finish very fast.

detail.text: The CPU is a computer's main chip: few cores, each good at complex work, so it still coordinates. GPUs were made to draw game graphics. AI's work is multiplying and adding huge tables of numbers, which splits into small pieces, so it suits a GPU.

prompts: Touch the watering can by the gardener
The gardener waters bed by bed. Now pull the bamboo valve on the crest
A thousand spouts at once. Now touch the watering can by the gardener to compare

scaling.label: More shovels, steady growth
scaling.art: A long stone seesaw resting on a mossy boulder, a jar standing on each end: Data on the left, Model size on the right. A sapling stands in the middle of the seesaw against the moon; a bamboo pipe with a turning handle lets a thread of silver drops fall to its foot. Beyond the mist, Gopher, a thick-trunked tree with a thin crown, stands on a knoll: its Model size jar overflows, its Data jar is nearly dry.
prompts: Turn the bamboo tap to add compute
Tilt the seesaw until both jars are even
scaling.tapAria: Bamboo tap handle: each turn multiplies compute by 10
scaling.beamAria: Stone seesaw: use the arrow keys to tilt it toward the Data jar or the Model size jar
scaling.lopsided: The {name} jar is short: lower that end

insights.text: Each tenfold of compute raises the tree one even step. With results that predictable, companies keep buying more chips.
With the same water, the tree that splits it evenly grows taller than the one that pours it all into size: a moderate model that reads more is more efficient.

detail.text: In 2022 DeepMind tested it: Chinchilla, a model 4 times smaller that read more text, beat Gopher on the same compute. The AI world calls these “scaling laws”.

moat.label: The moat round the castle
moat.art: Seen from high above, a round disc floating in the night: in the middle, NVIDIA's three-roofed stone castle on its island; round it, a black moat crossed by bamboo bridges you can count, out to a village. One village house is tied to the castle wall by five bridges. On the far lake, three boats with paper lanterns, Google's, Amazon's and AMD's, wait by three canals.
prompts: Drag a house to a rival's boat
Tap each bridge to cut it
Drop the house on the boat
moat.moatLabel: CUDA · programming tools that run only on NVIDIA chips
moat.houseAria: A village house, that is an AI programming team: drag it to a rival's boat

insight.text: Each bridge is code already written for CUDA, programming tools that run only on NVIDIA chips. Switching chips means tearing down the bridges and writing it again.

detail.text: The moat is deep, but it can be crossed. Anthropic uses Google's TPUs, Amazon's Trainium and NVIDIA GPUs alike. OpenAI has also signed for chips from Amazon and AMD.
Oct 2025: Anthropic announced it will use up to a million Google TPU chips in 2026.
Feb 2026: in its new funding round, OpenAI agreed to run part of its compute on Amazon's Trainium chips.
Oct 2025: AMD and OpenAI signed a GPU deal of about 6 gigawatts (measured by the power the chips draw); the first batch starts in the second half of 2026.

goldrush.label: Gold-rush season
goldrush.art: A long black ridge cut from paper runs across the lower part, a giant moon behind it that you drag through the years. Each milestone is a lamp post on the ridge; diggers with lanterns, the AI companies, climb in ever greater numbers toward NVIDIA's tent on the summit, where it sells the shovels (chips); beside it two heaps of gold stand in true proportion.
goldrush.prompt: Drag the moon through the years
goldrush.sliderAria: Drag the moon through NVIDIA's years

fact.text: Fiscal 2023 (to Jan 2023): NVIDIA sold $15.0 billion of chips to data centres, the buildings full of machines that run AI.
NVIDIA becomes the first company worth more than $5 trillion on the stock market.
Fiscal 2026: NVIDIA sold $193.7 billion of chips to data centres, nearly 13 times the figure three years earlier.
The latest quarter alone (report of 26 Aug 2026): $89 billion, more than double the same quarter a year before.

horizon.text: Some investors predict NVIDIA will be the first $10 trillion company; nobody knows how long the boom will last.

insight.text: In three years, NVIDIA's chip sales to data centres grew almost 13 times: the shovel seller gets paid first.

detail.text: In fiscal 2026 about 9 in 10 dollars of NVIDIA's revenue came from chips for data centres.

loop.label: The money loop
loop.art: Looking up from below the axle at a great wooden waterwheel beside NVIDIA's stone mill, against the moon. A stone flume carries water, the money, from the wheel's tail round the lake past the AI company's island (a pavilion with a lamp) and the data centre's (a row of stone lanterns), then over the mill roof back onto the wheel. At the last step two water marks appear on the mill wall: $22 and $51 billion.
loop.prompt: Tap or drag the waterwheel round, the way the arrow points
loop.wheelAria: The waterwheel: tap it, drag it round its axle, or press Enter, to turn it a quarter
flow: NVIDIA invests in an AI company
The AI company builds data centres
The data centres buy NVIDIA chips
NVIDIA's revenue rises, so it has more to invest

facts.text: Feb 2026: NVIDIA put in $30 billion of the $110 billion OpenAI had just raised.
In the first six months of 2026, what NVIDIA owns in companies not yet on the stock market grew from $22 billion to $51 billion.
Aug 2026: NVIDIA promised to repay up to $105 billion of debt if the company building data centres for OpenAI cannot.

view.text: It is circular investment, true, but if it works, customers will be tied tightly to NVIDIA.
NVIDIA sells the chips and also promises to repay its chip buyers' debt; that makes it all the more contested.
NVIDIA's money is only part of what customers raise; calling it “circular” is baseless.
Oct 2025: AI companies' share prices look too high; the risk of a sharp fall is growing.

common.text: The money really does go round. The debate: does it keep customers loyal, or inflate a value that could burst?

insight.text: The money NVIDIA puts into customers comes back as money spent on NVIDIA chips. The faster the wheel turns, the bigger the revenue.

loop.circlePrompt: Tap each stone: keeping customers, or a bubble?

detail.text: When you read “NVIDIA invests in X”, ask: does X buy NVIDIA chips?
